description: OrbitNsukka is a Nsukka-based team of five building an Astronaut Health Monitor, designed to work even with unreliable power and internet. We have ML/Python, C++/Qt, full-stack and agentic-AI skills, and a leader who loves maths and React. We’re looking for a designer or someone with health-science knowledge. Join us and learn by building.
summary:
StellaVita is an offline health check for astronauts on long missions, where help from Earth can be minutes away. The astronaut enters six everyday readings by hand: heart rate, blood pressure, blood sugar, body temperature, sleep hours and mood. None needs an invasive test. For each reading the app shows a status as a colour and a word (Normal, Caution or Emergency), the reason, and the published source behind it. It also watches for patterns across days, such as three short nights of sleep in a row.

Every range, rule and source lives in one threshold file that the app reads, so no health number is hidden in the code and each one can be traced to where it came from. Each indicator is also linked to the five hazards of human spaceflight, using NASA's published risk diagrams.

The app runs in a browser, works with no internet after its first load, and keeps all data on the device. It gives guidance, not a diagnosis: a red reading means contact the flight surgeon. StellaVita answers the challenge by giving crews a simple, cited way to check their own health when Earth cannot answer quickly.
details:
1. What does it do, and how does it work?
    StellaVita is a progressive web app. An astronaut picks a profile and enters a reading for any of six indicators: Heart rate: from a device or counted by hand. Blood pressure: two readings a minute apart; the latest is judged and both are kept. Blood sugar: before a meal only, with the meter used. Body temperature: with the method used. Only the mission's agreed method is compared with the ranges. Sleep: hours slept. Mood: a daily 1 to 5 tap, a weekly two-question check (the PHQ-2), and an "I am in severe distress" button. Symptoms are ticked from a short list with each reading. For every reading the app gives one result: a status (Normal, Caution or Emergency), the reason, and the source IDs behind the rule. It then looks back over earlier days for patterns: three nights of six hours' sleep or less, low mood on several days, or high readings that repeat. The app is built around one file, Indicator_Thresholds.json. It holds every range, symptom rule, pattern rule, input limit and source ID. The engine reads that file and nothing else, so a range can be corrected without touching the code. A test fails if any number from the file is typed into the app.
  2. A reading that is missing or impossible is never given a colour. The app asks again. If the same unusual value is entered twice, it is accepted and judged, so a real emergency is never blocked by a safety check. What benefits does it have? It works without Earth. After the first load it needs no internet, so it suits a mission where messages are delayed. Every number is cited. A crew member, a flight surgeon or a judge can follow any result back to its source. It is easy to read under stress. Three plain words, each with a colour and a symbol, never colour alone. It respects fit crews. An astronaut whose resting heart rate is normally low is judged against their own usual range. It is private. Readings stay on the device. There are no accounts, servers or tracking. It is honest about its limits. It is guidance only, and it says so on every screen.
  3. What is the intended impact? On the way to the Moon and Mars, crews will have to notice health problems early and act before Earth can advise them. StellaVita shows one way to do that with readings a crew member can take without a medical procedure. The same design, with its ranges kept in a separate file, could later serve clinics and communities with poor internet and power, which is our team's own daily situation.
  4. How is the project creative?
    A health tool you can audit. Each range carries its source ID, and values with no published source are openly labelled "team choice". One rulebook, read by two programs. The app's engine and an independent Python checker both read the same file and must agree on all 720 results in the demo data. Hazards linked to readings. Each indicator is linked to the five hazards of spaceflight and rated A, B or C by how directly NASA's Human System Risk Board diagrams connect them. Safety that doesn't get in the way. "Ask again, then accept" stops typing mistakes without hiding a true emergency. A name with meaning. Stella vita means "star life". What factors did our team consider? Non-invasive entry. The crew should not need a blood draw or a lab to use the tool. Power and internet. Our own outages shaped an offline-first design. Privacy and age. All team members are under 18, so the project uses no names, faces or voices, and only synthetic data. Scientific honesty. NASA's in-flight crew thresholds are not fully public, so our ranges are Earth adult values from public clinical sources, and the tool says so. Team decisions on record. Every rule in the tool traces to a numbered decision in our decision log, including the votes. Licences. Copyrighted sources are cited and linked, never copied. Our own work is released under the Apache License 2.0. Scope. The six indicators came first. Charts, reminders, a body figure and a radiation layer were set aside until the core worked. Use of AI We used AI tools, as the challenge allows, and we label where.
  5. Use of SI
    Claude (Anthropic), through Claude Code: research leads, drafting our documents, writing the threshold file from our decisions, the synthetic data script and checker, and the application code and tests. Z.ai: the first two drafts of our science pack, which we then reviewed and corrected. The team chose the challenge and the indicators, voted on the rules, decided every entry in the decision log, and signed the threshold file. The AI is never treated as a source: every health claim points to a published source. Every AI-generated file says so in its text or metadata, and the app's About screen shows the same notice. No NASA logos, flags or mission identifiers were used or generated.
